title: Reciting in prayer
hook: a short surah after the Fatiha in the first two units

segments.voice: Yesterday we turned around and saw Juz' 'Amma whole: the Day, the orphan, the soul, the One. Your line was the whole juz'. Which three surahs made your list? Day two hundred twenty-three.

The back of a mosque at sunset. The imam's voice rises: first the Fatiha, the seven verses said in every prayer. Then a pause, and something else. Tonight it's a surah about daybreak. Tomorrow it might be the one about the elephant, or the orphan, or the soul. Around the room, some who couldn't order lunch in Arabic follow every word, because they learned these short surahs as children. That's where Juz' 'Amma lives. Not on a shelf. In the mouths of people praying, all over the world. Today: reciting in prayer, and why this little part gets said so often.
screen: `SUNSET, AT THE BACK OF A MOSQUE.` → `THE FATIHA, THEN SOMETHING ELSE.` → `WHERE JUZ' 'AMMA LIVES.`

segments.voice: Each prayer is made of units, rak'ahs: standing, bowing, prostrating, sitting. In every unit, standing, the one praying recites the Fatiha. The Prophet Muhammad ﷺ said, in a hadith Bukhari records, that there is no prayer for the one who doesn't recite the opening of the Book. Then, in the first two units, something is added: a short surah, or a few verses from anywhere in the Qur'an. In the third and fourth units, the Fatiha alone. The schools of law weigh the addition differently: the Hanafi school counts it as required, and the others count it as a strongly recommended practice of the Prophet. At dawn, sunset and night, the imam recites aloud in the first two units; at noon and afternoon, silently. So people need a store of short surahs, and Juz' 'Amma is the store. Two stories show the spirit of it. One: a companion named Mu'adh led his people in prayer with such a long surah that a tired man left. The Prophet corrected him and named shorter ones instead, like By the sun and By the night. Two: another man, leading prayer, always added Say, He is Allah, the One, every single time. People mentioned it to the Prophet. Asked why, he said it describes the Most Merciful, and he loved to recite it. The Prophet said: tell him that Allah loves him. In that report, a short surah said with love is answered with love.
screen: `THE FATIHA IN EVERY UNIT.` · `A SHORT SURAH IN THE FIRST TWO.` · `MU'ADH IS TOLD: KEEP IT SHORTER.` · `THE MAN WHO LOVED AL-IKHLAS.` · then, large: `A NEW ONE TONIGHT.`

segments.voice: Sit, and choose one short surah you don't yet know by heart. Al-Kawthar has only three verses; so does Al-'Asr. Read it slowly in whatever language you have, then read it again. On each breath, take one line and let it settle. If you pray, you can say it after the Fatiha in one of tonight's prayers, even if it comes out slowly and you need to glance at it. If you don't, you can simply listen to it recited once today. The bell holds the time.
Reciting in prayer. The Fatiha in every unit, and a short surah after it in the first two, which is why Juz' 'Amma is heard so often. Today's word.
Your line: a new one tonight. Pick one short surah you've never said in prayer, or never heard aloud, and let tonight be its first time. Day two hundred twenty-three.

howItsDone: In each unit of the prayer Muslims recite al-Fatiha, and in the first two units they add a short surah or some verses, often from Juz' 'Amma; the imam recites aloud at dawn, sunset and night, and silently at noon and afternoon.

fork.setup: a man leading prayer adds Say, He is Allah, the One, every time. people complain. what does the Prophet say?
options: tell him to vary his surahs
tell him that Allah loves him
tell him to stop leading prayer
fork.reveal: the man said he loved it because it describes the Most Merciful. the Prophet said: tell him that Allah loves him (Bukhari).

original.note: Arabic: one unit of the prayer, named for the bowing (ruku').

trapdoor: what you thought: Muslims recite the same words every prayer.
what it means: the Fatiha is fixed, but the short surah after it changes, often drawn from Juz' 'Amma.
what a scholar hears: Bukhari 756 (no prayer without the Fatiha); Hanafis make the added surah wajib, the other schools sunnah; Bukhari 7375, the man who loved al-Ikhlas.
